amendments.rule: A pronominal suffix aligns to the English pronoun that realizes it, which is usually a possessive or object pronoun: `מִינֵהוּ` → *his kind* splits into the noun and *his*. **Where the ASV's paraphrase realizes one suffix twice, both pronouns belong to that suffix's one possibly discontinuous unit; an earlier realization does not make the later one `added`.** `מִכֶּם מָזוֹר` → *cure you of your wound* gives *you ... your* to the suffix and heads on *you*, the direct pronoun rather than the possessive recasting. **Where the ASV intensifies a possessive with *own*, the whole emphatic possessive belongs to the suffix:** `דְּרָכֶיךָ` → *thine own ways* gives *thine own* to the suffix and *ways* to the noun, headed on *thine*; do not attach *own* to the host noun merely because it stands beside it. **Where the ASV replaces the suffix's ordinary pronoun with a lexical nominal expression naming its referent, that whole expression realizes the suffix and the supplied lexical antecedent is not `added`; head on the noun or name that carries the referent.** `נְחָלֶיהָ` → *the streams of Edom* gives *of Edom* to the suffix and heads on *Edom*, and the suffix in `בִּסְעִיפֶיהָ הַפֹּרִיָּה` → *in the outmost branches of a fruitful tree* takes *of a tree*, headed on *tree*, while the adjective keeps *fruitful*. **An independent personal pronoun the ASV renders the same way goes with it.** Where a written subject or object pronoun is realized not by an English pronoun but by a demonstrative with a supplied lexical noun naming its referent, that whole expression realizes the pronoun and the supplied noun is not `added`; head on the noun carrying the referent: `הִיא הַסִּיר` → ***this city*** *is the caldron* gives *this city* to `הִיא`, exactly as rule 20's identifying formula gives *These ... that* to a `הוּא`, and an ASV italic on the supplied noun corroborates it without deciding it, by rule 7. Where the referent's own noun stands written in the clause, the pronoun takes only the determiner the ASV writes for it and the article is `unrepresented` under rule 41's limit: `הִיא נִתְּנָה הָאָרֶץ` → ***this*** *land* *is given*. **Where the ASV expands an object suffix into a full nominal expression containing a pronoun, the whole expression may realize the suffix, but the target head remains the pronoun that directly realizes the suffix's lexeme:** `אֲשִׁיבֶנּוּ` → *I will turn away the punishment thereof* gives *the punishment thereof* to the suffix and heads on *thereof*, not on the generic noun *punishment*. All eight occurrences of this prophetic formula across Amos 1–2 follow that analysis. **An English relative pronoun may be what realizes a suffix.** Where the ASV recasts the suffix's own clause as a relative clause modifying the noun its referent names, the relative — *that*, *which*, *who*, *whom* — is the pronoun the suffix is rendered by and joins its unit, exactly as rule 17 gives the *which* of such a recasting to an explicit subject pronoun, and whatever preposition the suffix stands on keeps only what the recasting leaves it under rules 40, 43 and 49: `שָׂרִים זָהָב לָהֶם` → *princes* ***that*** *had gold* gives *had* to the possessive `לְ` under rule 43 and *that* to the suffix, and `וַיָּסֶךְ אֱלוֹהַּ בַּעֲדוֹ` → *And* ***whom*** *God hath hedged in* gives *whom* to the suffix and leaves `בַּעַד` `unrepresented` under rule 40. Such a relative is not a subordinator supplied for the clause: rules 46 and 55 govern a clause with no morpheme in it to answer for the word, and here the suffix answers for it, so read whether a pronominal morpheme stands in the clause before marking a relative `added`. **And where the ASV supplies the antecedent noun as well as the relative, the two sentences above are one ruling and not two.** Where the suffix's clause is recast as a relative clause and the ASV writes a lexical noun naming the suffix's referent for that relative to modify, the noun and the relative together realize the suffix in one possibly discontinuous unit and neither word is `added`: `עָלֵימוֹ אָבַד כָּלַח` → ***Men*** *in* ***whom*** *ripe age is perished* gives *Men ... whom* to the suffix, discontinuous under rule 25 around the `עַל` that keeps its own *in*, and `לֹא עֹזֵר לָמוֹ` → ***men that*** *have no helper* gives *men that* to it while the possessive `לְ` keeps the *have* rule 43 gives it. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a noun: that ruling governs a noun supplied as the subject of a finite verb, and this one is the antecedent of a relative and answers to a suffix standing in the clause, so read what the supplied noun does before marking it. Head on the noun that carries the referent, as the sentences above head `הִיא הַסִּיר` → *this city* on *city* and `נְחָלֶיהָ` → *the streams of Edom* on *Edom*; the sentence heading an expanded object suffix on its pronoun governs a generic noun standing beside a pronoun that realizes the suffix directly — *the punishment thereof* — and a relative linking a recast clause to the noun that names the referent is not that. The competing head is the relative, so name it in the note under rule 8. Where no suffix or other possessive morpheme is present, a supplied possessive expression such as *your own* or *thine own* answers to no source morpheme and is `added` under rule 30. **The suffix on an infinitive construct is that infinitive's subject and takes the English subject pronoun the ASV writes for it**, while the infinitive keeps the verb: `עַד כַּלֹּתוֹ אֹתְךָ` → *until he have consumed thee* gives *he* to the suffix and *have consumed* to the infinitive, and the object marker and its own suffix are read separately by rules 16 and 11. The ASV's pronoun need not agree in number with the suffix — `עַד הַאֲבִידוֹ אֹתָךְ` → *until they have caused thee to perish* — because the English subject answers to the referent the translation has in view; align the pronoun that is written. This governs only a suffix that is actually present: where none is, a subject pronoun the ASV supplies for an infinitive belongs to the infinitive itself under rules 48 and 52, and rules 40 and 43 dispose of the other places where the English pronoun realizing a morpheme is neither possessive nor object.
amendments.why: JOB.30.2 and JOB.30.13 write the same construction — a 3mp suffix whose clause the ASV recasts as a relative clause with a supplied lexical antecedent — and the chapter analysed them two ways, marking *Men* `added` in one verse and giving *men that* whole to the suffix in the other. Rule 18 already contains both halves of the answer but never joins them: one sentence gives a supplied lexical antecedent to the suffix and heads on the noun, another heads an expanded object suffix on its pronoun, and rule 17's supplied-subject sentence looks as though it reaches a supplied noun of any kind. The amendment joins them, rules out rule 17 for a noun that is an antecedent rather than a subject, fixes the head on the noun carrying the referent with the relative named as the competing head, and leaves every existing sentence of rule 18 in place. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad reading is corrected where a later pass will meet it.

conventions: Where the ASV recasts a pronominal suffix's clause as a relative clause and supplies a lexical antecedent noun for it, the noun and the relative both belong to the suffix's unit and neither is `added`; head on the noun carrying the referent. JOB.30.2 gives *Men ... whom* to the מוֹ of עָלֵימוֹ, discontinuous around the *in* that stays with עַל, and JOB.30.13 gives *men that* to the מוֹ of לָמוֹ while the possessive לְ keeps its *have*. Heading such a unit on the relative was the competing reading in both.

This chapter's verb renderings head on the lexical verb wherever the second English word is a directional particle — *cast off*, *thrust aside*, *set forward*, *poured out*, *passed away*, *stand up*, *bindeth about*, *gathered together*, *lift up* — and on the second word only where it is a predicative complement carrying the Hebrew verb's own lexeme: JOB.30.10 heads רָחֲקוּ → *they stand aloof* on *aloof*, because *stand* alone names posture and *aloof* alone names the distance רָחַק means. The two shapes look alike in the dump and the line between them is rule 44's, not a difference of policy.

report: One genuine cross-verse split, and the candidate table could not show it because half of it is an `added` unit. JOB.30.2 and JOB.30.13 are the same construction — a 3mp suffix מוֹ whose clause the ASV recasts as a relative clause, with a lexical antecedent *men* supplied for it. JOB.30.13 gave *men that* whole to the suffix under rule 18; JOB.30.2 gave only *whom* to the suffix and marked *Men* `added` under rule 17. Nothing in the source licenses the difference: a suffix stands in both clauses and the ASV supplies a noun naming its referent in both. Rule 18 says in terms that such a supplied antecedent is not `added`, so JOB.30.2 is patched to match JOB.30.13 — the suffix takes *Men ... whom*, discontinuous around the *in* that stays with עַל, headed on *Men*. Rule 17's `added`-subject sentence does not reach it, since *Men* is not the subject of a finite verb.

Candidates checked and found source-licensed rather than split. מֵעַל is fused in both JOB.30.17 (*in*) and JOB.30.30 (*from*), each headed on מִן, which is what rule 23 directs for one construction the ASV renders with different prepositions. מִפָּנַי fuses to *before* in JOB.30.11 but splits in JOB.30.10, where the ASV writes *in ... my face*: rule 30's one-rendering condition is met in the first and unmet in the second. אִם takes the fronted auxiliary in JOB.30.25 (*Did ... Was*, distributed under rule 25) but not in JOB.30.24, where the ASV has already written *Or* for it — rule 17's second limit and rule 51.

The `added` units were read end to end, since the table is blind to them. A preposition supplied to reach a verb's own object joins the verb in JOB.30.16, 30.26 and 30.27, while JOB.30.14 and 30.22 supply preposition and pronoun together and are `added` — that is rule 44's own division, not a split. Supplied possessives with no suffix present are `added` alike in JOB.30.12, 30.18 and 30.24; supplied connectives with no waw present are `added` alike in JOB.30.28 and 30.30; supplied prepositions on nouns the Hebrew writes go to the noun alike in JOB.30.3, 30.6, 30.17, 30.22 and 30.23, while JOB.30.5 supplies the noun as well and is `added` under rule 33's closing sentence.

Heads were checked verse by verse. Nine verb-plus-particle units head on the lexical verb (*cast off*, *thrust aside*, *set forward*, *poured out*, *passed away*, *stand up* twice, *bindeth about*, *gathered together*, *lift up*), and JOB.30.10 heads *stand aloof* on *aloof* instead. That is not a split: *aloof* is a predicative complement carrying רָחַק's lexeme of distance, as *heavy* does in rule 44's *made heavy*, whereas *off*, *aside*, *up* and *together* name nothing alone. Logged as a convention so it is not re-litigated.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The five R disagreements (JOB.30.1 עַל, 30.2 לְ, 30.3 the second בְּ, 30.9 לְ, 30.13 לְ) are the documented convention difference — four are rule 40 recastings that leave the preposition no English word, and the fifth is a repetition rule 22 leaves unrendered. The paragogic nun at JOB.30.17 is rule 32 as written, and its packet gloss *rest* is a distribution defect under rule 39. The unrepresented waw at JOB.30.26 is right: the ASV opens that apodosis with the presentative *there*, which rule 17 gives the verb, and writes no connective. JOB.30.25 יוֹם is a judgment call the verse already named under rule 8 — קְשֵׁה־יוֹם split with יוֹם unrepresented rather than fused, because *trouble* carries קָשֶׁה's sense and not יוֹם's; the accepted edge stands.

One amendment returned, to rule 18. The rule has one sentence giving a supplied lexical antecedent to the suffix and another heading an expanded object suffix on its pronoun, and this chapter met the case that engages both at once. The amendment says the two are one ruling where the ASV supplies antecedent and relative together, fixes the head on the noun carrying the referent, and states that rule 17's supplied-subject sentence does not reach such a noun.
